recipes.title: Herb Roasted Turkey Breast
recipes.blurb: All the good parts of Thanksgiving without wrestling a twenty-pound bird — a bone-in breast, herb butter under the skin, and two hours in the oven. It feeds six and slices beautifully.

items: 1 bone-in, skin-on turkey breast (5 to 6 lb / 2.3 to 2.7 kg)
1 large yellow onion (about 2 cups / 280 g), cut into thick rings
2 medium carrots (1 cup / 130 g), cut into 2 in (5 cm) pieces
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) low-sodium chicken or turkey stock

instructions.title: Thaw completely
instructions.text: A frozen 6 lb (2.7 kg) breast needs about 24 hours in the refrigerator to thaw, so plan a day ahead. Roasting a partially frozen breast guarantees a dry outer inch and an undercooked center. Press the thickest part with your thumb — it should give evenly with no hard core.

instructions.title: Dry and salt the breast
instructions.text: Pat the turkey bone dry with paper towels, then mix the kosher salt with the baking powder and rub it over all the skin and into the underside. Set it on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 4 hours, or up to 24 if you can. The baking powder raises the skin's pH so it browns faster, and the dry fridge air dehydrates the surface for crisper results.

instructions.title: Make the herb butter
instructions.text: Mash the softened butter with the sage, parsley, rosemary, thyme, garlic, and lemon zest until it is uniformly green-flecked. Keep it at room temperature so it is spreadable but not melted — melted butter will not stay where you put it. Taste a small amount; it should be assertively herbal, since it has a lot of mild meat to season.

instructions.title: Butter under the skin
instructions.text: Slide your fingers between the skin and the meat, starting at the wide end, and work carefully to loosen the whole surface without tearing it. Push about two-thirds of the herb butter into that pocket and press from the outside to spread it evenly over both lobes. Rub the remaining butter over the outside of the skin and grind the black pepper over the top.

instructions.title: Come to room temperature
instructions.text: Leave the buttered breast on the counter for 45 minutes before it goes in the oven. Turkey breast is a thick, dense piece of lean meat, and starting it cold means the outside overcooks by 20°F before the center reaches temperature. This one step meaningfully improves how juicy the finished slices are.

instructions.title: Heat the oven to 425°F
instructions.text: Set a rack in the lower-middle position and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). You will start hot to set the skin and then drop the temperature, which gives you color without drying out the meat. Give the oven a full 20 minutes after it beeps so it is truly saturated with heat.

instructions.title: Build the vegetable rack
instructions.text: Scatter the onion rings and carrot pieces across the bottom of a roasting pan or a large oven-safe skillet, then set the turkey breast skin-up directly on top of them. The vegetables lift the meat so hot air circulates underneath and they keep the drippings from scorching on the bare pan. Pour 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the stock into the pan around them.

instructions.title: Roast hot, then drop the heat
instructions.text: Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 20 minutes to set and start browning the skin, then reduce the oven to 350°F (175°C) without opening the door. Continue roasting for 60 to 75 minutes more, depending on size — figure roughly 15 minutes per pound at the lower temperature. If the skin browns faster than you like, lay a loose sheet of foil over the top.

instructions.title: Temp in the right place
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the breast, parallel to the bone and not touching it, and look for 160°F (71°C) if you are resting it or a full 165°F (74°C) if you are not. Carryover cooking will add 5 to 10°F (3 to 6°C) during the rest, which is why pulling at 160°F (71°C) and resting is the reliable way to hit 165°F (74°C) without overshooting. Check in two places, since one lobe is often thicker.

instructions.title: Rest 20 minutes
instructions.text: Move the breast to a carving board and rest it for a full 20 minutes, loosely tented only if your kitchen is cold. A large piece of meat needs this long for the juices to redistribute, and cutting early will flood your board and leave the slices dry. Use the time to make the gravy.

instructions.title: Make the pan gravy
instructions.text: Set the roasting pan over medium heat, pull out the vegetables, and whisk the flour into the fat and drippings, cooking for 2 minutes until it smells toasty. Pour in the remaining 1 cup (240 ml) of stock in a slow stream while whisking hard, and simmer for 4 to 5 minutes until it coats a spoon. Take it off the heat, swirl in the cold butter, and taste before adding any salt — the drippings are already seasoned.

tips: Make ahead: salt the breast up to 24 hours in advance and make the herb butter up to 3 days ahead. On the day, it is mostly hands-off oven time.
A boneless rolled breast works too but cooks faster — start checking at 60 minutes total and pull at the same 160°F (71°C) before resting.
Save the bone. Simmered with an onion and a bay leaf for 3 hours it makes stock that turns leftover turkey into an excellent soup.
Leftover slices keep 4 days and are best reheated gently in a covered pan with a splash of stock, which keeps them from turning to sawdust.
Dried herbs can stand in at one-third the volume, but fresh sage and rosemary really do make the difference here.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull the breast at 160°F (71°C) and rest 20 minutes; carryover brings it to a safe 165°F (74°C). Never serve poultry below 165°F (74°C).
recipes.pairing: A dry Riesling or Pinot Noir, with mashed potatoes, buttered green beans, and plenty of the pan gravy.

recipes.title: Chicken Cordon Bleu
recipes.blurb: Pounded chicken breast rolled around ham and Gruyère, breaded, seared, and baked until the cheese pulls in strings when you cut it. Fussy in the best way, and genuinely impressive on a plate.

items: 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts (6 to 7 oz / 170 to 200 g each)
8 thin slices Black Forest or good deli ham (about 6 oz / 170 g)
6 oz (170 g) Gruyère cheese, cut into 4 batons
2 large eggs, beaten with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water
1/4 cup (60 ml) neutral oil, for searing
1 small shallot (about 1/4 cup / 35 g), finely minced

instructions.title: Butterfly the breasts
instructions.text: Lay each breast flat and, holding your knife parallel to the board, slice horizontally through the thick side almost but not all the way through, then open it like a book. Work slowly and keep your guiding hand flat on top of the meat. If a breast has a tenderloin attached underneath, pull it off and save it for another use, since it will not roll cleanly.

instructions.title: Pound them thin
instructions.text: Place each butterflied breast between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the center outward with a mallet or a heavy pan until it is an even 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Use glancing, spreading blows rather than straight-down smashes, which tear holes. Any hole in the meat is a hole the cheese will escape through, so patch tears by overlapping the edges.

instructions.title: Season and spread
instructions.text: Season both sides of each pounded breast with the kosher salt and black pepper, then spread a thin layer of the 2 tsp Dijon over the inside face. The mustard adds a sharp note that cuts the richness and it also helps the ham stick to the meat. Do not oversalt — the ham and Gruyère are both already salty.

instructions.title: Layer the filling
instructions.text: Lay 2 slices of ham on each breast, leaving a clear 1/2 in (1 cm) border on all sides, then set a baton of Gruyère along the short edge nearest you. That border is critical: filling that reaches the edge will push out and leak in the pan. Cut the cheese into batons rather than using slices so it sits in a compact log.

instructions.title: Roll them tight
instructions.text: Starting from the cheese end, roll each breast up as tightly as you can, tucking the sides inward as you go like a burrito. Wrap each roll snugly in plastic wrap, twisting the ends like a candy wrapper to compress it into a firm cylinder. Chill the wrapped rolls for at least 30 minutes so they hold their shape when they hit the breading station.

instructions.title: Set up the breading
instructions.text: Put the flour in one shallow dish, the beaten eggs in a second, and the panko tossed with the melted butter and 1/2 tsp salt in a third. Buttering the panko is what lets it brown deeply in the oven without needing a deep fry. Keep one hand for dry and one for wet so you do not end up with breaded fingers.

instructions.title: Bread the rolls
instructions.text: Unwrap a roll, dredge it in flour and tap off every bit of excess, dip it in the egg and let the drips fall away, then press it into the panko, packing crumbs on firmly all over. Set it seam-side down on a rack. Excess flour is the usual reason breading falls off in the pan, so be thorough about that tap.

instructions.title: Chill again
instructions.text: Refrigerate the breaded rolls uncovered on the rack for 15 to 20 minutes while the oven heats to 375°F (190°C). This second chill sets the coating so it stays on during searing and firms up the rolls so they hold their cylinder. It also gives the panko time to absorb a little moisture and adhere.

instructions.title: Sear all sides
instructions.text: Heat the 1/4 cup oil in a 12 in (30 cm) oven-safe skillet over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the rolls seam-side down and sear for about 2 minutes per side, turning to hit all four faces. It should sizzle steadily and the panko should turn deep golden; if it browns in under a minute, the pan is too hot. Use two spatulas or tongs and turn gently so the coating stays intact.

instructions.title: Bake to temperature
instructions.text: Transfer the skillet to the 375°F (190°C) oven and bake for 15 to 18 minutes. If your skillet is not oven-safe, move the rolls to a rack set over a sheet pan instead, which keeps the bottom from going soft. The rolls will firm up noticeably and you may see a little cheese bubbling at a seam, which is fine.

instructions.title: Check the center
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of a roll, through the side and into the chicken rather than the cheese pocket, and look for 165°F (74°C). Chicken breast has no fat to protect it, so pull them the moment they arrive. Rest the rolls on a rack for 5 minutes before slicing so the molten cheese sets just enough to stay put.

instructions.title: Make the Dijon cream
instructions.text: Pour the oil out of the skillet, add the 1 tbsp butter, and cook the shallot over medium heat for 2 minutes until translucent. Pour in the wine, scrape the bottom, and reduce it by half, about 3 minutes, then add the cream, Dijon, thyme, and salt. Simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until it coats a spoon, and taste before adding more salt.

instructions.title: Slice and serve
instructions.text: Cut each roll crosswise on a slight diagonal into three or four thick slices and fan them on the plate so the ham and cheese spiral shows. Spoon the sauce onto the plate underneath rather than over the top, which keeps the panko crisp. Serve immediately, while the cheese still stretches.

tips: Make ahead: assemble and bread the rolls up to 24 hours in advance and keep them uncovered on a rack in the fridge. Sear and bake straight from cold, adding 3 to 4 minutes in the oven.
Gruyère is traditional and melts beautifully, but Emmental, Comté, or a good Swiss all work. Avoid pre-shredded cheese, which is coated in starch and melts gummy.
The number one failure is cheese leaking out. The fixes are a clean 1/2 in border, a tight plastic-wrap roll, and a full 30-minute chill before breading.
For a fully crisp shell, shallow-fry the rolls in 1/2 in (1 cm) of oil at 350°F (175°C) for 3 minutes per side and skip the searing step, then bake 12 minutes.
These freeze well breaded but unbaked. Freeze on a tray, bag them, and bake from frozen at 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 40 minutes to 165°F (74°C).
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the chicken at the center of the roll reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer.
recipes.pairing: A dry white Burgundy or Alsatian Pinot Blanc, with buttered egg noodles and a bitter greens salad.

recipes.title: Chicken Satay with Peanut Sauce
recipes.blurb: Turmeric and lemongrass marinated chicken threaded onto skewers, grilled hard and fast, and dunked in a peanut sauce with real body. Great as dinner, even better as something to hand people standing in a kitchen.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 in (2.5 cm) strips
1 cup (240 ml) full-fat coconut milk, well shaken
1 stalk lemongrass (about 3 tbsp), tender core finely minced
3/4 cup (200 g) natural creamy peanut butter
1/4 cup (60 ml) hot water, to loosen
16 bamboo skewers (8 in / 20 cm), soaked 30 minutes
1/4 cup (35 g) roasted peanuts, roughly chopped

instructions.title: Cut the chicken for skewers
instructions.text: Slice the thighs with the grain into strips about 1 in (2.5 cm) wide and 4 in (10 cm) long so they can be threaded and will not fall apart. Cutting with the grain rather than across it gives strips that hold together on a skewer. Keep the thickness even at about 1/2 in (1 cm) so they grill in the same amount of time.

instructions.title: Prep the lemongrass
instructions.text: Trim the dry top and root end off the lemongrass stalk, peel away the tough outer layers, and mince only the pale, tender bottom 4 in (10 cm) as finely as you can. Lemongrass fibers stay woody no matter how long you cook them, so the fineness of the mince genuinely matters. If you cannot find fresh, use 1 tbsp of lemongrass paste or the zest of one lime.

instructions.title: Mix the marinade
instructions.text: Whisk the 1 cup coconut milk, fish sauce, brown sugar, lemongrass, garlic, ginger, turmeric, coriander, cumin, and kosher salt until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is a uniform bright yellow. Turmeric stains everything it touches, so keep it off wooden spoons and light countertops. It should smell fragrant and savory rather than sharply fishy — the fish sauce mellows completely once cooked.

instructions.title: Marinate 2 to 12 hours
instructions.text: Turn the chicken strips in the marinade until coated, cover, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours and up to 12. Coconut milk marinades are gentle and there is no acid to worry about, so a long soak here only helps. Give the container a shake once partway through.

instructions.title: Soak the skewers
instructions.text: Submerge the bamboo skewers in water for at least 30 minutes, weighing them down with a plate so they stay under. Dry bamboo catches fire over direct heat and you will end up with half a skewer and chicken in the coals. Metal skewers skip this step entirely and are worth buying if you do this often.

instructions.title: Make the peanut sauce
instructions.text: Warm the peanut butter, 1 cup coconut milk, fish sauce, lime juice, brown sugar, soy sauce, and red curry paste in a small saucepan over medium-low heat, whisking constantly for 4 to 5 minutes. It will look separated and grainy at first and then suddenly come together into a smooth, glossy sauce. Whisk in hot water 1 tbsp at a time until it pours slowly off the spoon like heavy cream.

instructions.title: Taste and balance
instructions.text: Taste the sauce and adjust it against four points: salty from the fish sauce, sour from the lime, sweet from the sugar, and hot from the curry paste. It should taste slightly too intense on its own, because it will be eaten in small amounts alongside mild chicken. Set it aside off the heat, where it will thicken as it cools — loosen it again with hot water before serving.

instructions.title: Thread the skewers
instructions.text: Weave each strip of chicken onto a skewer in a loose S-shape, pushing it down to leave about 2 in (5 cm) of bare skewer at the handle end. Do not pack the meat tight against itself, because the pressed surfaces will steam instead of char. One or two strips per skewer is right for 16 skewers.

instructions.title: Get the grill hot
instructions.text: Heat a charcoal grill until the coals are covered in white ash, or a gas grill to high, aiming for a hot direct zone around 450°F (230°C). Scrub and oil the grate just before cooking. If the exposed skewer ends worry you, lay a folded strip of foil along the edge of the grate and rest the handles on it.

instructions.title: Grill hard and fast
instructions.text: Lay the skewers over direct heat and grill for 3 to 4 minutes per side, turning once, until the edges char and the surface looks lacquered. The coconut milk and sugar in the marinade brown quickly, so stay at the grill and move any skewer that is coloring too fast to a cooler spot. Total time is only 6 to 8 minutes — this is not a walk-away dish.

instructions.title: Check, then serve hot
instructions.text: Probe the thickest piece on a skewer for at least 165°F (74°C); thigh meat this thin usually gets there right as the char develops. Pile the skewers on a platter, scatter the cilantro and chopped peanuts, and serve with the warm peanut sauce, lime wedges, and sliced cucumber alongside. The cucumber is not decoration — its coolness is what lets you keep eating.

tips: Make ahead: the peanut sauce keeps 1 week refrigerated and the chicken can marinate up to 12 hours. Reheat the sauce gently with a splash of water, since it sets firm when cold.
Use natural peanut butter with no added sugar or palm oil. The sweetened kind makes a cloying sauce you cannot balance back.
Chicken breast works if you slice it thin and pull it at exactly 165°F (74°C), but thighs stay far juicier over high heat.
No grill? Broil the skewers 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 4 minutes per side, or cook them in a hot cast-iron grill pan in two batches.
Double the peanut sauce and keep the extra for noodles, roasted broccoli, or as a dressing thinned with lime juice and water.
